div.head: Chapter 30
div.p: This conclusion with all its parts is proved by this single reason alone, namely: because these later men, and those later still, committed the very same as those before. Indeed experience shows that each new band that came distinguished itself in being more cruel. Therefore the same reasoning applies to these as to those, and thus by all the proofs of law brought forward to condemn those men, these are condemned.
But so that this may be more easily seen, let us point to the passages where each part of the conclusion is proved.

The first part says that they were public enemies of those commonwealths: because, those commonwealths and kingdoms being free and secure in their own kingdoms and lands, as was proved in the first principle, they entered killing and robbing and subjugating and placing in servitude all the peoples they passed through, without having done them any injury or harm, as is manifest. It is the work of enemies and mortal adversaries to rob and kill and destroy commonwealths and the lives and states of their inhabitants, and to usurp the possessions of those who are their enemies. Although in truth, they are more properly plunderers, robbers, and brigands than enemies: for all the evils, destructions, and harms they have done were without the authority of the kings of Castile, on the contrary all against their express commandments and through their own wickedness, ambition, and greed, as appears above in chapter 18 and those following. For enemies are properly those against whom open or public war is waged by command of the prince. All of this is proved by the L. hostes, Digest., De captivis et postlimino and in L. hostes, ff., De verborum significatione. And so they are properly plunderers, robbers, brigands, and thieves, as those laws state.
That they are tyrants, see the first principle, the second § 4, and §§ 24 and 15.

That they committed most grave mortal sins: this will be manifest from the proof of the first conclusion to the first doubt. Especially — setting aside the robberies and killings — in having divided the towns among themselves, despoiling the natural kings and lords of their states, dignities, lordships, honors, and jurisdictions, and of their vassals and subjects, revenues, and royal rights, placing them in the most vile, abased, and contemptible state that any lord who had fallen from his position was ever seen to be in. And all — subjects and lords alike — they placed in the harshest servitude that is the repartimiento, where, occupied in the violent services and tributes imposed on them, they cannot devote themselves to hearing the preaching and doctrine of Christ; and in which they finally perish both spiritually and bodily. All of this appears above in §§ 16 and 17. Therefore they sinned most gravely.

That for the robberies of gold and silver and emeralds and other jewels and precious things and livestock, and the harms they did while engaged in those raids, they are bound to restitution, not only each one for himself but in solidum: this has been made evident in §§ 24 and 25.

Of the other thousands, so numerous and great, which after the robberies they committed along the way, and after subjugating the peoples so violently and tyrannically as has been said, they acquired through the outrageous tributes: it might appear at first sight that they were not bound to restore them in solidum, but that each one was bound to restore what he had received from the towns that fell to him in the said repartimiento. But, considering that one man or a few would not have dared to subjugate those peoples with such great cruelties, nor to make the said repartimiento among themselves, if they had not all gone together; and being all of one same will and all pursuing the same end: it is manifest that all of them were the total cause, not only of what was robbed and the evils they did while going about robbing, subjugating, and killing peoples, but were also the total cause of the said repartimiento and of the evils and harms that arose from it for the Indians; and consequently of the tributes that each one robbed from the towns that fell to him. Therefore all are bound in solidum to restore everything that each one and the others so tyrannically and impiously obtained, even if it be a single grain of maize. That the lands and estates which in New Spain are called milpas and in Peru chácaras they are bound to restore to them: of this not even the most dull and barbarous will be in doubt. The reason for this is: that just as they unjustly robbed the treasures and all the other moveable things from their proper owners and were tyrants in doing so, in the same way they usurped the lands and estates from the kings and particular lords and were tyrants in doing it. And consequently, if they are bound to restore moveable things, they are still more bound to restore immoveables and real property, because the reason for this is greater than for those. And so they could not take even a span of land without grave mortal sin, nor can they hold it as their own without being condemned, because they committed theft and violence or rapine, unless the Inca kings whose those kingdoms are were to forgive them graciously, or some particular owner wished of his own free will to give it to them. This appears above, § 23, in the fourth proof of the first part of the first conclusion.

From this it follows that all the public buildings of cities, towns, and places, and those that private persons built, and the estates, vineyards, and orchards they planted, and the livestock pastures: stand on foreign soil and land, whether of the said Inca kings or of private individuals, and all are held by us tyrannically and we are possessors in bad faith; and this unjust possession will never be justified unless the Inca kings or their heirs and the private owners grant them to us graciously; rather everything built is lost to us, for it was the lords, kings, or their subjects who owned the ground on which it was built. First, because the building regularly passes with the soil, as in Inst., De rerum divisione, § Cum autem in suo. Second, because one who builds on another's soil knowingly and in bad faith — as we Spaniards — loses the part of his thing — namely, the materials if he provided them — and is said to commit a wrong: Inst., same title, § ex diverso et § qua ratione. Bartolus, in L. in rem, § sed si alias, § si quis rei, ff., De reinvindicatione. And it can be destroyed by the sole authority of the owner of the soil: Bartolus and the Doctors, in L. sed si inter, ff., De servitute urbanorum praediorum; et in L. quemadmodum, ff., Ad L. Aquiliam, § 17. And the building must be demolished at the cost of the one who built illicitly. And this is on the assumption that they themselves built it at their own cost and with their own hands — how much more so since everything was built by the Indians at their own cost and with their labor, constrained and forced against all reason and natural law, just as the children of Israel built the cities in Egypt, subjected by force by the tyrant Pharaoh!

The final clause of the conclusion, namely, that those peoples have just war or the right to wage it against those who came later, as against the first, just, continuous, and perpetual: this is sufficiently made manifest in § 26 and those following. And let this be the resolution of the second doubt.
